transcript.content: Hi, I’m glad you came in. What brings you in today?

Well, I guess... I mean, I didn't really decide to come here on my own, they kind of made me. It’s all because of work, down at the freight warehouse. I started there after I took some time off from my college classes, just moving material, loading pallets, that kind of thing. But it’s... the guys on the floor, the foreman, they just don't understand what I'm doing and they get so worked up about it. 

I guess they brought me in because I keep doing things out there by the loading dock. Like, I’ll be right next to the forklift, and I just... I freeze. I'll just stop completely, with my arms straight up in the air by the machine, and I just hold it there. It's like I'm stuck like that. And when the trucks or the lifts are moving, I start copying the sounds, making the exact beeping noises they make when they back up, and doing all the hand signals the spotters use, just over and over and over again. 

And the boxes... they just want them stacked straight, but I've been moving them in these strange little patterns. It’s like they have to go in these specific shapes, shifting them around into this exact design on the floor. I'll be right in the middle of doing it, getting the pattern right, and everyone on the floor is just yelling and screaming for me to stop, telling me I'm holding up the whole freight line. But I just... I don't stop, I just keep doing the patterns even with them yelling at me and waving their arms. So the foreman pulled me off the floor and, well, that's why they brought me here.
When you were a child, did you often do repetitive movements or get very focused on arranging things in specific patterns?

No, no, I... I don't think so. I mean, my mom always said I was a pretty normal kid, you know? I liked playing outside, riding my bike down the hill by our old house, the one with the big oak tree in the front yard. I didn't really care about how my toys were set up. I just threw them in the bin when I was done. I mean, sometimes I'd build forts out of pillows and blankets, but that was just normal kid stuff, right? Everyone does that. I didn't... I didn't have to have things a certain way. I just played. 

It's just now, at the warehouse, it's different. The boxes, they just... they feel wrong if they aren't in the shapes. But back then, no, I never did anything like that. I was just a regular kid, going to school, playing tag at recess, eating peanut butter sandwiches. I didn't have any rules about how things had to look or anything. I don't know why it's happening now, with the boxes and the sounds. It's just... it's just the warehouse, I guess. It's the warehouse that makes it happen. But no, not when I was little. Not at all.
Have you had any recent seizure, head injury, or serious medical illness?

No, I... I haven't had anything like that. No seizures or anything. I mean, I've never even fainted in my whole life, not even when I had to get my blood drawn for that physical before I started at the warehouse. The nurse said some guys my size, you know, they just keel right over when they see the needle, but I was totally fine, just watched the tube fill up. And no head injuries either. I mean, sure, when I was a kid I fell off my bike a couple of times, scraped my knees up pretty bad on the gravel driveway at that house with the oak tree, but I always wore my helmet. My mom was really strict about the helmet, it was this bright blue one with a little visor on it. She’d always check the strap before I could ride down the hill. So, no concussions or anything where I hit my head hard. 

And as for being sick... no, nothing serious. I had a cold a few weeks ago, just a regular runny nose and a little bit of a cough, but I took some over-the-counter stuff and drank a lot of orange juice, the kind with extra pulp, and it cleared right up in a few days. I didn't even miss a shift at the warehouse for it. I've never been in the hospital for anything, never had any surgeries or weird infections. I'm generally pretty healthy, I think. I try to eat okay, you know, not too much fast food, though sometimes the guys at work want to grab burgers on the lunch break and it's hard to say no. But yeah, physically, my body is fine. It's just... it's just the stuff at the loading dock, the way I get stuck and the patterns with the boxes. But nothing is actually wrong with my health, like a disease or a brain injury or anything like that. I'm sure of it.
Have you had a period where you felt extremely high, energized, or unusually irritable for days at a time?

No, no, nothing like that. I haven't had any days where I felt like I was on top of the world or full of energy, or where I was just snapping at everyone. I mean, sure, sometimes I'm tired after a long shift at the warehouse, because moving those pallets and stacking the boxes, even when I'm doing the patterns, it takes a lot out of you, you know? And sometimes the guys on the floor can be annoying, like when they leave their empty energy drink cans right on the edge of the loading dock where they could fall and get crushed by the forklift tires. That bugs me a little, but it doesn't make me angry or irritable for days. I just pick up the can and throw it in the recycling bin by the breakroom door. 

I'm pretty even, I guess. I just wake up, have my bowl of cereal—usually the frosted flakes, I like how the milk gets sweet at the end—and I go to work. I don't get these big bursts of energy where I feel like I could run a marathon or stay up all night painting the house or whatever it is people do when they feel like that. I just do my job, or try to, until the foreman starts yelling. But even when he yells, I don't get mad back at him. I just... I just keep doing the patterns with the boxes or making the sounds. I don't feel high or energized, I just feel like I have to do what I'm doing. So, no, no days like you're talking about. Just regular days, mostly.
During this time, have you been feeling very depressed most of the day nearly every day?

No, I... I don't think depressed is the right word at all. I mean, I don't feel sad or heavy or anything like that. You know how when people are depressed, they just want to lay in bed all day and they cry or they don't want to eat? Like when I was taking a few classes at the community college before I dropped out and started working full-time at the warehouse, my roommate got really depressed because his girlfriend broke up with him, and he wouldn't even get up to go to the dining hall for pizza on Fridays, which was his absolute favorite. He just laid there staring at the ceiling fan. 

But I'm not like that. I get up every morning the second my alarm goes off at 5:30. I take a shower, I have my cereal, and I walk down to catch the 42 bus right on the corner. It drops me off a couple of blocks from the loading dock, and I just walk the rest of the way, usually just looking at the cars going by. I'm not walking along feeling down or hopeless or like life is terrible. I just... I just go to work. 

And even when things get stressful there, like when the foreman gets on my case and starts shouting about me being too slow because I'm making sure the boxes are in the right shapes, I don't go home and cry about it. It doesn't hurt my feelings. I just go home, maybe microwave some macaroni and cheese—the kind with the white cheddar, it tastes a little better than the orange kind—and sit on the couch and watch whatever is on TV. I don't feel sad. It's really just that my mind is so busy with the boxes and the sounds and making sure the patterns on the pallets are exactly right. It takes up all my focus, you know? So there isn't really any room to feel depressed or anything like that. I'm just doing what I have to do at the warehouse.
While all of this has been happening, have you had times when your mood felt normal, but the freezing, copying sounds, or box-patterning still kept happening?

Well, I mean, my mood is always pretty normal, I think. Like I was just saying, I don't get super high or super low. I'm just... I'm just me. Just regular. So, yeah, all the time, basically. When I'm at the warehouse and I get stuck, like when I'm standing by the conveyor belt and my body just won't move, or when I have to arrange the boxes so the barcodes are facing a specific way—like, they have to form a square, and if it's not a perfect square, I have to start over, even if the foreman is yelling at me to hurry up and get the pallet wrapped—my mood is totally fine. I'm not sad or angry or anything when that happens. 

And the sounds, too. When I hear the forklift backing up, that *beep beep beep*, and I just have to make the exact same sound back, right out loud, *beep beep beep*, at the same pitch and the same speed... I'm not feeling weird emotionally when I do it. I just feel normal. It's just that I *have* to do it. It's like my brain is telling me the pattern has to be completed, the sound has to be matched, but my mood is just... flat, I guess. Or not flat, just regular. Like how you feel when you're just standing in line at the grocery store waiting to pay for your milk. You're not happy, you're not sad, you're just there. That's how I feel when all this stuff is happening. It's been happening a lot, actually, the freezing and the sounds, pretty much every shift now, but my mood hasn't changed at all. It's just my body and the boxes and the noises that are doing all this stuff. I feel completely normal inside, like mood-wise.
About how long has the freezing, copying sounds, and arranging boxes in patterns been going on?

Well, it's been... let's see. It's been going on for a while now. I'd say about six months, maybe a little more, but definitely around six months. I remember because it started right around the time the weather started getting really cold, back in late October or early November. I had just bought this new heavy winter coat from the surplus store downtown—the one with the deep pockets and the thick lining, because the warehouse gets freezing in the winter since the loading dock doors are open all the time. And I was standing there, wearing the new coat, and that was the first time I got stuck. I was trying to reach for a box of automotive parts, and my arm just stopped mid-air, and I stood there for what felt like ten minutes, just staring at my own hand. The foreman thought I was messing around. 

And then the sounds started a few weeks after that, right around Thanksgiving. I remember because the guys in the breakroom were talking about turkey and stuffing, and someone dropped a metal thermos on the concrete floor, and it made this loud *clack-ping* sound, and I just repeated it, *clack-ping*, right out loud, completely automatically. And since then, it's just been happening more and more. The box patterning really picked up after Christmas, when we had all those returns coming in and there were so many different sizes of boxes. I just couldn't put them on the pallets normally anymore. They had to be in the right shapes. So yeah, it's been about six months of all this... this confusing talking and the freezing and the sounds and the boxes. Six months of it happening almost every day at the warehouse. It's really taken over my whole shift, honestly, ever since I bought that winter coat.
Have you been hearing voices when no one else is around?

Voices? No, no, I don't hear any voices. Just the regular sounds, you know? The warehouse sounds. Like the forklift backing up, or the pallets dropping, or the conveyor belt squeaking. I mean, there's always noise at the warehouse, but it's not voices talking to me when nobody is there. It's just... well, sometimes the guys talk, obviously, like when they're yelling across the dock to get someone's attention, or when they're complaining about the schedule in the breakroom. Usually they're complaining about the new supervisor, Dave, who always schedules people for closing and then opening the next day. It's called a "clopen," they say. I don't mind it so much because I just get up at 5:30 anyway, but they really hate it.

But when I'm alone? Like when I walk home or when I'm just sitting in my apartment eating my white cheddar macaroni and cheese? No, it's just quiet. Well, except for the TV, or maybe the hum of the refrigerator. My refrigerator has this really specific hum, it goes *mmm-hmmm-mmm*, and sometimes I catch myself making that sound back, just like I do with the forklift. But it's not a voice. It's not someone talking to me or telling me things or anything like that. I just hear the normal things that are actually there, and then my brain just... makes me copy them. But definitely no voices. I think I'd be really scared if I started hearing people talking when my apartment was empty. It's just me and the refrigerator hum.
Do you believe someone or something is controlling your actions?

Controlling my actions? Like, like someone else is making me do things? No, no, I don't think so. It's not like there's a guy with a remote control or some kind of microchip in my brain, you know? I've seen movies like that, where the government or aliens are steering people around like video game characters, but that's not what this is. It's just... it's just my own brain, I think. It's my brain getting stuck. Like a record player that hits a scratch and just keeps skipping on the same note over and over. 

When I freeze up at the conveyor belt, it's not because someone is holding me there. It's just that I... I can't find the next movement. Like the signal from my brain to my arm just gets lost somewhere in the wires. And with the boxes, the patterning, it's me doing it. I know I'm doing it. I'm the one looking at the barcodes and making sure they line up into a perfect square. It's just that I feel this intense pressure that it *has* to be done that way, otherwise it's wrong. It's like an itch you have to scratch, but it's in my head. 

And the copying sounds, too. When I hear the forklift and I go *beep beep beep*, it's my mouth making the sound. It's not someone else talking through me. It's just... automatic. Like when a doctor hits your knee with that little rubber hammer and your leg kicks out. You didn't decide to kick, but it's still your leg doing it, right? Nobody is forcing your leg, it's just a reflex. That's what it feels like. A really complicated reflex that makes me arrange boxes and repeat the refrigerator hum. But it's all me. Just a very stuck, very glitchy version of me. So no, I don't think anyone is controlling me. It's just my own body doing these weird things on its own.
Have these freezing spells, sound-copying, and box-patterning been happening continuously for at least one month?

Well, continuously? Like, every single day without stopping? I mean, I guess it depends on what you mean by continuously. If you mean, has there been a whole month where this stuff happens every day, then yes, definitely. Like I said, it's been going on for about six months total, since I bought that winter coat, and it's definitely been happening every single day for way more than a month. 

I mean, I go to work at the warehouse five days a week, Monday through Friday, usually the 6:00 AM to 2:30 PM shift, unless Dave makes me do a clopen, which like I said, I don't really mind, but the other guys hate. And every single shift, without fail, I freeze up at least once. Usually it's by the conveyor belt when the smaller packages come down, the ones from the online retailers that are all wrapped in that gray plastic instead of cardboard. I'll just be standing there, and my hand goes out to grab one, and then... nothing. I just stop. And it's not just a quick pause, it's a real freeze. The other day, I think it was Tuesday, or maybe Wednesday—no, it was Tuesday because they were serving meatloaf in the cafeteria—I froze for so long that a whole line of packages backed up and fell off the end of the belt. The supervisor was yelling, but I couldn't move. 

And the sounds, too. That happens every day. Like the forklift backing up, the *beep beep beep*, or the scanner going *boop*. I do it all the time. Even on the weekends when I'm not at work, I'm doing it at home with the refrigerator, the *mmm-hmmm-mmm*. Or if a car drives by my apartment and honks, I'll honk back, out loud. So yeah, it's not like it takes a break. It's not like I have a week where I'm totally fine and then a week where it comes back. It's every day. It's been every day for months now. 

And the boxes... well, that's every time I have to load a pallet, which is constantly. I can't just throw them on there anymore. I have to find the corners, I have to match the barcodes, I have to make the shapes. And if I don't, if someone else tries to help me and puts a box in the wrong spot, I have to take it off and do it again. So it's definitely continuous. It's a constant, everyday thing that just... it just doesn't stop. It's like my brain is stuck in this loop, every single day, for way more than just one month. It's been a solid block of this since the weather got cold.
Before these problems started, had you been having trouble keeping up with school, work, or other daily responsibilities?

Before? Oh, no, before all this started I was doing fine. I mean, I was busy, but I was handling it all. It was only after this whole stuck-brain thing started that everything went downhill. Because now... well, now it is just a mess. 

Like at the warehouse, I actually used to drive the forklift. That was my main thing, and it was great because you get to sit down and just steer the pallets around, which is a lot easier on your feet. But I lost my forklift duties entirely. Dave, the supervisor I told you about, he pulled me aside and said I was a liability. He told me people were saying they could not keep things safe around me anymore because I would just stop moving in the middle of the loading dock, or I would be making the backup beeps with my mouth instead of actually paying attention to where I was driving. So they took the keys away and put me back on the floor, which is why I am always standing at the conveyor belt now.

And it is not just work. I was taking classes at the community college, just trying to get my general education credits done so I could maybe get a degree later on. I had this history class on Tuesdays and Thursdays, and the professor always wore these really thick wool sweaters
Did these problems begin very suddenly, over a few days?

Suddenly? Like, I just woke up one morning and couldn't move my arms? No, no, it wasn't like that at all. It wasn't just a few days where everything went crazy all at once. If I really think about it, the whole thing... it's actually been a really long time coming. Things have really been going downhill for about 11 months now. 

Yeah, 11 months. That was right around the time I moved into this shared apartment. I was trying to be smart about things, you know? I wanted to be closer to work at the warehouse and closer to the community college, because before that, I was taking the bus from way across town. It was like a forty-five-minute ride each way, sometimes an hour if the traffic was bad, which it always is on Thursdays for some reason. So I found this place, it's a four-bedroom apartment, and I moved in with these three other guys I didn't really know, just to cut down on the commute. I thought it was going to make my life so much easier and give me more time to study and sleep. 

But almost as soon as I unpacked my stuff in that new room—it's the one at the very end of the hall, right next to the bathroom, so I hear the pipes rattling all the time—that's when the downhill slide really started. It wasn't the full-on freezing at the conveyor belt right away, but it was just... things slipping. The pressure in my head starting to build up. I'd be trying to organize my new closet or set up my desk for school, and it would just take forever because things didn't feel right, or my thoughts would just start getting tangled up. 

So it definitely wasn't a sudden, over-the-weekend kind of
Have other people told you that your speech has become hard to follow or confusing?

Yeah, they do. They actually do say that. A lot, actually, especially lately. Dave, the supervisor I was just telling you about? He gets really frustrated with me about it now. 

Because, okay, so part of my job, even when I'm just on the floor by the conveyor belt and not driving the forklift anymore, is helping check the staging lanes. And Dave will come up to me with his clipboard—he always has this heavy metal clipboard with the big clip at the top that snaps really loud—and he'll ask me which pallets are going on the outbound truck. The 3:00 PM truck, usually. Which should be a really simple question, right? It's just pointing to a lane. But when I open my mouth to answer him, to just tell him what's going on, it's like my words just completely slip off the track. 

I start trying to explain it to him, but then my words just jump. I'll be talking about the load sheet, the yellow carbon copy one we use for outbound freight, but then something about it just jumps my brain over to my old house. The one I lived in before I moved into this new apartment with those three guys. And suddenly I'm telling Dave about the old house, and the garage out back, which makes me think about packing up the truck for fishing. Because we used to go fishing all the time, early in the morning, and you have to organize all the tackle boxes perfectly so the hooks don't get tangled. And then just talking about the tackle boxes... it jumps me over to the church boxes. Like, the big wooden donation boxes
At any time since this started, have you had a period of at least one week when you felt clearly depressed or unusually high?

Depressed? Or high? Like... like really happy or energetic? No, no, I haven't really had anything like that. Not for a whole week, definitely not. I mean, I'm not exactly thrilled about losing my forklift privileges, obviously. It's a huge bummer being stuck at the conveyor belt all day because it really does a number on your lower back. You're just standing there on that hard concrete floor, and they have these anti-fatigue mats, but honestly, they don't do anything. They're just these thin pieces of rubber with holes in them, and by the end of an eight-hour shift, my knees are just killing me. So yeah, I get down about that sometimes, because who wouldn't? 

But it's not like a deep, dark depression where I can't get out of bed or anything. I still get up. I still go to the apartment kitchen and make my oatmeal—I have the instant kind, the maple brown sugar one, because it's fast and you just need hot water from the kettle, which is good because one of my roommates, Greg, he always leaves his dirty dishes in the sink, so I can't even use a real pot to cook anything. 

And as for feeling unusually high or super energetic... no, definitely not that either. I don't get these big bursts of energy where I feel like I can conquer the world or stay up for three days straight. If anything, I'm just trying to keep my head above water with the warehouse and the community college classes. Well, the classes I was taking, anyway. The history one with the professor in the thick wool sweaters. He actually wears them even when the heater in the building is cranked all the way up, which I never understood. It's got to be at least eighty degrees in that lecture hall, and he's up there in this heavy, scratchy-looking maroon sweater, just talking about the Industrial Revolution. 

But no, to answer your question, my mood hasn't been stuck way up high or way down low for a week or anything like that. It's just... I'm just trying to get through the days with everything else going on, you know? The stuck-brain feeling and the words jumping tracks. That's the main thing. My mood is just... normal, I guess. Normal for someone dealing with all this.
Have you found yourself caring much less than usual about things, like losing motivation or interest in work, school, or seeing other people?

Caring less? Losing motivation? I mean... I wouldn't say I've lost interest or stopped caring about things, not really. It's not like I just don't care anymore. It's more like... well, take the warehouse, for example. Like I said, I'm stuck at the conveyor belt now, right? And I still go, I still show up for my shifts, even though it's super repetitive and my back hurts. I still care about doing the job, it's just harder to do it now with my brain getting stuck and the words jumping around when Dave asks me questions. But I still want to do a good job, you know? I want to get my forklift privileges back eventually. I haven't just thrown in the towel on that. 

And with school... well, the community college classes. I haven't stopped caring about them either. I mean, I was talking about that history professor, the one with the maroon wool sweater? I actually really liked that class. I thought the Industrial Revolution stuff was pretty interesting, especially how it changed all the factories and the way people worked, which kind of made me think about the warehouse and how we use the conveyor belts now instead of just carrying everything by hand like they probably had to do back then. I still care about learning all that. It's just that it got so hard to concentrate with the pressure in my head, and my thoughts getting all tangled up when I tried to read the textbook. The textbook was this massive, heavy thing, too—like, literally heavy, it must have weighed five pounds, and the pages were that really thin, glossy paper that reflects the light from my desk lamp right into my eyes. 

But I didn't lose interest in it. I didn't just wake up and say, 'I don't care about history anymore.' It's just that the other stuff, the slipping and the freezing, got in the way. 

And as for seeing other people... I mean, I live with three other guys now. I see them every day. Well, mostly I just see Greg leaving his dirty dishes in the sink, or I hear the other two playing video games through the wall. They play these first-person shooter games, and they have the bass turned way up on their TV, so I can feel the explosions vibrating through the floorboards when I'm trying to study or sleep. But I don't avoid them because I don't care about them. I'm just... I'm just dealing with a lot right now. So I might stay in my room a bit more, the one at the end of the hall by the rattling pipes, just to try and keep my head straight. But it's not because I've lost motivation to have friends or anything. I just... I haven't really noticed a drop in how much I care. It's just harder to do the things I care about.
When you freeze and hold your body in one position, does that posture stay fixed even if someone tries to move you?

Well, if someone tries to move me... I mean, I guess that's actually the whole reason they brought me in here in the first place, to be honest. Because at the warehouse, I keep doing these things where I just... I get stuck. Like, I'll be standing right by the forklift—not driving it, like I said, just near it on the floor—and I'll just freeze with my arms up in the air. Just stuck like that. And I don't even know if they try to push my arms down or move my body because mostly they just start yelling at me right away. 

But while I'm frozen there with my arms up, I start copying the sounds the forklift makes. You know that really loud, piercing backup alarm? That OSHA safety thing? The *beep, beep, beep*? I just start making that exact sound out loud, over and over, and I'll start copying the hand signals the spotters use for the drivers when they're backing into the tight staging lanes in aisle four. I just keep doing the signals and the beeping while I'm frozen.

And it's not just the freezing and the beeping, either. When I'm back at the conveyor belt, I'll start taking the boxes—the heavy corrugated cardboard ones with the yellow shipping labels—and instead of pushing them down the line, I keep moving them into these strange little patterns. Like, arranging them so the corners touch in a specific way, making these little geometric shapes on the concrete floor, over and over. And Dave and the other guys will be standing right there, literally yelling at me, just screaming for me to stop and get back to work, but I just... I just keep doing it. The patterns and the freezing and the beeping, even with everyone yelling. So I guess that's why they made me come talk to you.
Have you been speaking much less than usual?

Speaking much less? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean, you can probably tell I'm talking plenty right now, right? I definitely haven't lost my words or stopped talking to people. If anything, I feel like I'm constantly having to explain myself to everyone, probably more than I used to. 

Like with Dave at the warehouse... I'm always trying to tell him why the boxes have to go in those specific shapes, those geometric patterns on the floor that I was just telling you about. I'll stand there and explain the whole system to him, how the yellow shipping labels need to face a certain direction so the barcodes catch the overhead scanners properly. Because the scanners on line four have been acting up since last Tuesday when maintenance tried to fix the belt motor, and they just left this big grease stain on the concrete that nobody bothered to mop up. So I talk to him about it, I try to explain my reasoning and how the corners of the boxes have to align, even if he is just yelling at me to get back to the conveyor belt. 

And with my roommates, too. I definitely haven't stopped talking to them. Just yesterday, I had a really long conversation with Greg about the sink situation. I explicitly told him that I just need enough space to put my ceramic mug under the faucet to get hot water for my oatmeal. Because, like I said, I eat the maple brown sugar instant kind, and if his crusty plates from his late-night pizza rolls are piled all the way up to the spout, I can't even get the water in the mug without the bottom of it touching the gross, dried-up tomato sauce and the cheese crusts. So I explained all that to him, in a lot of detail, probably for like ten or fifteen minutes straight while he was just sitting there on the couch trying to play his shooter games with the bass turned all the way up. 

So no, I'm definitely still talking. My voice works fine, the words come out... well, sometimes they jump tracks in my head, like I said before
Do you believe people at work are trying to harm you or are plotting against you?

Harm me? Plotting against me? No, no, I don't think anything like that. I mean, I know I said Dave and the other guys yell at me a lot, but they aren't trying to hurt me or secretly conspiring against me or anything. It's not a plot. It's just... well, it's a warehouse, you know? They have these really strict daily quotas they have to meet. If the corrugated boxes don't get down the conveyor belt and loaded into the freight trucks by 4:00 PM, the whole supply chain gets backed up, and then the regional manager comes down from the upstairs office and gets on Dave's case. 

So when Dave is standing there screaming at me to stop making the geometric patterns on the floor and get back to work, his face gets all red—like, right up to the rim of his plastic safety glasses, the ones with the little scratch on the left lens that he's always rubbing at with his shirt—but he's just stressed out about the shipping metrics. He's not trying to harm me. 

Actually, the whole place is very strictly regulated for safety anyway. We all have to wear steel-toed boots and those bright neon orange high-visibility vests with the reflective silver strips, and there are OSHA posters everywhere in the breakroom, right next to the vending machine that's always out of the peanut butter crackers I like. So nobody is going to physically hurt me there. The only thing that hurts is my lower back from standing on that hard concrete all day, and maybe my eyes from the overhead fluorescent lights that have that constant, low buzzing sound. But as far as the other guys go, no, they definitely don't have the time or the energy to plot against me. They're just trying to get their hours in. They just want me to stop doing the backup alarm noises and push the boxes down the line so everybody can clock out and go home.
When you freeze in one position, if someone tries to move your arm, does it stay where they place it?

Well, see, that's the thing, I don't really know if they move my arm or not, because like I was trying to say before, when I get stuck like that, freezing by the forklift, they don't usually come up and physically touch me. They mostly just stand there yelling. Like Dave, he'll just be standing there with his red face, yelling at me to stop. 

But if they did try to move my arm... I don't know, maybe it would stay? I really couldn't tell you for sure. Because when I'm doing it, when I'm frozen with my arms up in the air, I'm just so focused on the whole situation, you know?
